unit.unitOverview: This unit is about keeping a conversation going. You will ask questions that open a subject up. You will make a suggestion and answer one. You will also learn eight verbs that carry a small word with them, and where the object goes.
unit.learningPath:
Meet 30 words for talking, suggesting and working with people.
Read a conversation, an information page and a community notice.
Ask questions that open a subject up: What do you mean by that?
Suggest something with what about and how about.
Use look after, put off and deal with, and place the object correctly.
Choose as or like to say how.
Say what two people do for each other.
Speak, write, take the quiz, then record your assignment.

visual.lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 15. This unit is about keeping a conversation going.
You can already ask a question and give an answer.
The problem comes next. The answer stops, and nobody knows what to say.
This unit gives you the sentence that comes after the answer.
Start with eight verbs that carry a small word with them.
Look after means take care of a person, an animal or a thing.
Put off means move something to a later time.
Deal with means take a problem and handle it.
Carry on means keep going.
Give up means stop doing something you used to do.
Find out means learn a fact you did not know.
Turn down means say no to an offer.
Take over means start doing the job somebody else was doing.
The small word is part of the verb. Put off has nothing to do with putting.
Now the words for the talk itself.
When you mention something, you say it quickly, in passing.
When you explain something, you make it clear how or why.
When you describe something, you say what it is like.
When you respond, you answer what the other person said.
When you interrupt, you start talking before the other person has finished.
When you clarify, you say the same thing again in clearer words.
When you summarise, you say a long thing again in a few words.
When you comment, you say what you think about something.
Next, the people.
A partner is a person you work with, or the person you live with.
A team is a small group working towards the same result.
A member is one person inside a group.
A community is the people who live or work in one place.
A relationship is the way two people are connected.
A contact is a person you can call when you need something.
A stranger is a person you have never met.
An acquaintance is between the two. You know them a little, but not well.
Last, the words for suggesting.
A suggestion is an idea you offer.
An option is one of the things you could choose.
An alternative is the other way, for when the first way does not work.
A proposal is a plan you put to a group, often in writing.
When you recommend something, you tell somebody it is good.
When you volunteer, you offer to do something before anybody asks you.
Now the patterns.
The first pattern is the question that opens a subject up.
A closed question gets one word back. Did you go? Yes.
An open question gets a sentence back. How did it go?
Keep five ready. What do you mean by that? How did that go? What happened next? Why do you say that? What was it like?
The second pattern is the suggestion.
What about and how about take a noun, or a verb with -ing.
What about tea? How about starting now? What about the late bus?
Never put to after them. Not: how about to start.
The third pattern is where the object goes.
Look after and deal with keep their small word beside them. Look after her. Deal with it.
Put off, give up, find out, turn down and take over can split.
You can say put off the call, or put the call off. Both are correct.
But when the thing is it or them, the small word goes last. Put it off.
The fourth pattern is as and like.
As gives the real job, or the real use. She works as a nurse.
Like says it is similar, but not the same. It looks like rain.
The fifth pattern is each other.
We help each other means I help her and she helps me.
One another means the same thing. It sounds a little more formal.
Work through the cards, then record yourself.
Every answer is in the unit, so you can always check your own work.

readings.title: The lesson Ana kept putting off
readings.setting: The step outside a block of flats
readings.passageScript:
Ana and Tomas live in the same block. Ana is sitting on the step. Tomas comes past with the shopping.

Tomas: You look tired. How did the lesson go?
Ana: It did not go. I put it off again.
Tomas: What do you mean by that?
Ana: I have put it off three weeks running. Every Tuesday something comes up. This week I had to look after my sister's little boy.
Tomas: And what happened next?
Ana: Nothing happened. That is the problem. I keep saying I will carry on, and then I do not.
Tomas: Can you tell me more about the lesson itself? Is it the lesson you do not like, or is it the Tuesday?
Ana: The Tuesday. I finish work at six and the lesson starts at six.
Tomas: So you are saying the time is wrong, not the lesson.
Ana: Yes. I had not put it that way before.
Tomas: Then what about the Thursday group? How about asking whether they still have a place?
Ana: I did not know there was one.
Tomas: Find out. Do not give up on the whole thing because one evening does not fit.
Ana: And if I am the last to arrive every week?
Tomas: Deal with that when it happens. One problem at a time.
Ana: You sound like my manager.
Tomas: I am saying it as a friend. Ask them tomorrow, and tell me what they say.

readings.title: Five ways to keep a conversation going
readings.setting: A page from a short guide for adult learners
readings.passageScript:
Most conversations do not stop because somebody is rude. They stop because nobody asks the second question.

One. Ask an open question.
A closed question gets one word back. An open question asks for a sentence. How did that go? What happened next? What was it like?

Two. Say back what you heard.
When you summarise, you say a long answer again in a few words. So you are saying the time is wrong, not the lesson. If you have it wrong, the other person will clarify, and you both move on.

Three. Ask somebody to explain.
Nobody minds being asked. What do you mean by that? is a short, polite sentence. It is better than nodding and hoping.

Four. Comment, then hand it back.
If you only respond with yes, the talk ends with you. Add a comment, then ask. That sounds difficult. How did you deal with it?

Five. Make a suggestion.
A conversation that reaches a problem needs somewhere to go. What about a later group? How about asking the team? A suggestion turns a complaint into a plan.

Two things to avoid.
Do not interrupt. Let the other person finish, even when you think you know the end.
Do not mention a person who is not there, unless you would say the same thing to their face.

None of this needs perfect English. A stranger becomes an acquaintance because you asked one more question, not because you used a long word.

readings.title: Riverside community group: notice for new members
readings.setting: A board inside a community centre
readings.passageScript:
RIVERSIDE COMMUNITY GROUP
Notice for new members

WHO WE ARE
We are a group of about forty members. We live or work in the same neighbourhood. Nobody is paid. Everybody volunteers.

WHAT WE DO
Three teams run at the moment.
Garden team: looks after the beds and the two benches. Meets Saturday morning.
Repair team: deals with small repairs for anybody who asks. Meets Thursday evening.
Welcome team: contacts every new household within a month.

HOW TO JOIN
Come to any meeting. You do not need to be a member first.
Each team works in pairs, so you will have a partner from your first day.
If Saturday does not suit you, there is an alternative: the garden team also meets on Wednesday at six.

MAKING A SUGGESTION
Any member may put a proposal to the group.
Write it on the form in the green folder by the door. Keep it under one page.
The group reads every proposal at the monthly meeting and answers within two weeks.
We turn down very few. When we do, we explain why and we recommend another way.

IF YOU CANNOT COME
Tell your team partner. Do not put it off until the day.
If you want to give up a team, say so and somebody will take over. Nobody is asked to explain.

CONTACT
Ask for the duty member at the desk. The desk is open from ten until four every weekday.

grammar.title: What do you mean by that? Opening a subject up
grammar.explanation: A closed question gets one word back: yes, no, a time, a name. An open question asks the other person to say more. Keep five open questions ready, and the talk does not stop after the first answer.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Closed: Did you go? - Yes.
Open: How did it go?
Closed: Is it far? - No.
Open: What is it like?
Five to keep ready:
What do you mean by that?
How did that go?
What happened next?
Why do you say that?
Can you tell me more about it?
The verb form comes before the subject:
did you go, does she know, is it far, was it busy, have you tried.
The same order follows what, how, why and when:
What did you do? How does it work? Why was it late?
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Somebody says: I put the appointment off.
A closed question stops the talk: Did you? Yes.
So pick an open one.
Ask what you do not know. You do not know why.
Start with the question word: Why.
The verb form comes next, before the subject: did you.
Then the rest: put it off.
Answer: Why did you put it off?
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to keep the ordinary order: Why you put it off? English moves the verb form in front of the subject here. Write: Why did you put it off?
grammar.memoryTip: One answer, one new question. Take a word out of their answer and ask about that word.
grammar.practice:
Write an open question for each answer.
1. Yes, I went. (ask how it went)
2. I deal with the post every morning. (ask what time)
3. She turned it down. (ask why)
4. We found out last week. (ask how)
5. It was busy. (ask what it was like)
6. I gave up in June. (ask what happened next)
7. A member of the garden team looks after the beds. (ask who)
8. I put it off. (ask what you mean)
grammar.answerKey:
1. How did it go? 2. What time do you deal with the post? 3. Why did she turn it down? 4. How did you find out? 5. What was it like? 6. What happened next? 7. Who looks after the beds? 8. What do you mean by that?
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: writing Why she turned it down. A question with why needs did in front of the subject, and then the plain verb: Why did she turn it down?
Item 7 looks wrong and is right. When the question word is the subject, nothing moves: Who looks after the beds? No did is needed there.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: What about a break? How about starting now?
grammar.explanation: What about and how about are the two quickest ways to suggest something. They mean the same. After them you put a noun, or a verb with -ing. You never put the word to.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
With a noun:
What about tea?
What about the late bus?
How about a shorter meeting?
With a verb and -ing:
How about starting at eight?
What about asking the team?
How about turning it down?
Saying yes: Good idea. That works for me.
Saying no, politely: I would rather not. Is there an alternative?
Not: How about to start at eight.
Not: What about we start at eight.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The problem: the meeting is too long.
Decide the suggestion: start it later.
Pick what about or how about. Both work.
Now choose the shape. Start is a verb, so it needs -ing.
That gives starting.
Put it together: How about starting later?
A noun works too: How about a later start?
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write How about to start? The word to never follows about. Use the -ing form: How about starting?
grammar.memoryTip: After about, a thing or an -ing word. Never a to.
grammar.practice:
Write a suggestion with what about or how about.
1. The room is cold. (close the window)
2. Your partner is tired. (a break)
3. The bus is late. (walk)
4. Nobody knows the price. (find out)
5. The team has no leader today. (Eva takes over)
6. The proposal is too long. (a shorter one)
7. You cannot meet on Monday. (Tuesday)
8. The job is too big for one person. (share it)
grammar.answerKey:
Model answers. Either opener is correct.
1. How about closing the window? 2. What about a break? 3. How about walking? 4. What about finding out? 5. How about Eva taking over? 6. What about a shorter one? 7. How about Tuesday? 8. What about sharing it?
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: writing How about to walk. After about the verb takes -ing: How about walking?
Item 5 is the hard one. A person can stand between about and the -ing word: How about Eva taking over?

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: Look after, put off, deal with: two words, one job
grammar.explanation: Some verbs carry a small word with them. The pair means one thing, and the meaning is not in the two words. Put off has nothing to do with putting. The only new question is where the other thing goes.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
These three keep the pair together:
look after: I look after my neighbour's cat. I look after her.
deal with: She deals with the post. She deals with it.
carry on: Carry on with the form. Carry on working.
Never: I look her after.
These five can split:
put off, give up, find out, turn down, take over.
I put off the call. I put the call off. Both are correct.
But with it or them, the small word goes last:
I put it off. She turned them down. We found it out.
Never: I put off it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: turn down, and the thing is the offer.
Ask: is turn down in the list that splits? Yes.
So both orders are correct.
I turned down the offer.
I turned the offer down.
Now change the offer to it.
With it, only one order is left.
Answer: I turned it down.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write I put off it. When the thing is it or them, it goes in the middle: I put it off. With look after and deal with nothing moves at all: I look after it.
grammar.memoryTip: Two lists. Look after, deal with and carry on never split. The other five split, and must split around it and them.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each sentence, changing the words in brackets to it or them.
1. I put off (the meeting).
2. She looks after (the two children).
3. We must deal with (this problem).
4. He turned down (the two offers).
5. They found out (the price).
6. Please carry on with (the list).
7. The team took over (the shop).
8. I gave up (coffee).
grammar.answerKey:
1. I put it off. 2. She looks after them. 3. We must deal with it. 4. He turned them down. 5. They found it out. 6. Please carry on with it. 7. The team took it over. 8. I gave it up.
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: writing She looks them after. Look after never splits, so the object stays after the pair.
Item 6 catches people too. Carry on with keeps both small words together: carry on with it.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: She works as a nurse. It looks like rain.
grammar.explanation: As gives the real job, or the real use of a thing. Like says that one thing is similar to another and is not it. One small word changes who somebody actually is.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
As, for the real job or the real use:
She works as a nurse.
He started as a cleaner and now he is the manager.
I use this box as a table.
I am telling you this as a friend.
Like, for similar but not the same:
It looks like rain.
She talks like a manager, but she is not one.
This drink tastes like tea.
He drives like somebody on his first day.
The test: put is between the two parts.
She works as a nurse, so she is a nurse.
She works like a nurse, so she is not one.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: My partner works (as / like) a teacher, and she is very good at it.
Ask: is she really a teacher?
The second half says she is good at it, so yes, that is her job.
A real job takes as.
Answer: My partner works as a teacher.
Change one word and the meaning turns over.
My partner works like a teacher means she has a different job.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write She works like a nurse when you mean the job. Like says she only seems similar to one. Write: She works as a nurse.
grammar.memoryTip: As is the truth. Like is the look.
grammar.practice:
Write as or like in each gap.
1. My neighbour works ____ a driver. That is her job.
2. The sky is grey. It looks ____ rain.
3. He started ____ a cleaner and now he is the manager.
4. This drink tastes ____ tea, but it is not tea.
5. I am telling you this ____ a friend, not as your manager.
6. She deals with problems ____ somebody who has done it for years.
7. We used the big box ____ a table.
8. The new member talks ____ a teacher, but he works in a shop.
grammar.answerKey:
1. as 2. like 3. as 4. like 5. as 6. like 7. as 8. like
The likeliest wrong answer is 6: writing as. She is not somebody who has done it for years; she only works in a similar way. Similar takes like.
Item 5 holds both words in one sentence. As a friend is what he truly is today, and as your manager is the other real job he is not using here.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: They help each other: one another too
grammar.explanation: Each other is for people who do the same thing to each other. I help her and she helps me becomes we help each other. One another means the same, and sounds a little more formal.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I help her. She helps me. Together: We help each other.
The two teams know each other well.
The members of the community look after one another.
The two partners email each other every morning.
A thing can follow it, with an apostrophe and s:
We know each other's names.
They took over each other's tasks for a week.
Careful: they help them means they help other people.
They help each other means the help goes both ways.
Each other never starts a sentence, and it never takes a plain s.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Two sentences: Eva calls Tomas every week. Tomas calls Eva every week.
Ask: is it the same action, both ways?
Yes. Eva to Tomas, and Tomas to Eva.
So one sentence can hold both.
Put the two people together as the subject: Eva and Tomas.
Keep the verb: call.
Finish with each other.
Answer: Eva and Tomas call each other every week.
One another is also correct, and a little more formal.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write They help each others. Each other never takes a plain s. Write: They help each other. The only s is the possessive one: each other's names.
grammar.memoryTip: Both ways, or it is not each other. Ask: does the action go from A to B and from B to A?
grammar.practice:
Join or repair each item, using each other or one another.
1. Ana helps Ben. Ben helps Ana.
2. The two teams trust the other team.
3. My partner and I call every evening. Make it clear it is both ways.
4. The members explain things to the other members.
5. Eva knows Tomas. Tomas knows Eva.
6. We know the names of each other. Use the possessive form.
7. The two neighbours look after the other one's cat.
8. Repair this: The two strangers talked to each others.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Ana and Ben help each other. 2. The two teams trust each other. 3. My partner and I call each other every evening. 4. The members explain things to one another. 5. Eva and Tomas know each other. 6. We know each other's names. 7. The two neighbours look after each other's cat. 8. The two strangers talked to each other.
The likeliest wrong answer is 6: writing each others' names. The apostrophe goes before the s, because each other counts as one thing: each other's.
Item 4 shows that one another is simply the more formal word. Each other is correct there too.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A short message
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a message of four sentences to somebody in a group you belong to. Say that you cannot come this week, and say what happens next. Use four of these verbs: look after, put off, deal with, carry on, give up, find out, turn down, take over. You may invent the group and the reason.
writing.modelText:
Hello. I cannot come on Thursday, because I am looking after my neighbour's little boy.
Please do not put the meeting off for me.
Eva said she would take over my part of the list this week.
I will find out about Saturday and let you know tomorrow.
writing.successCriteria: Four sentences. Four different verbs from the list, one in each sentence. Every sentence has a capital letter and a full stop. Where the thing is it or them, it sits in the middle: put it off.
writing.support: Do one sentence first. Choose the verb, then the thing, then decide whether the pair splits. Look after, deal with and carry on never split. Put off, give up, find out, turn down and take over do.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence with a suggestion: What about Saturday instead?

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 2 — Two people who work together
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write five sentences about two people who deal with each other every week. They can be two neighbours, two members of a team, or two people at work. Use each other or one another twice. Use as once for a real job, and like once for something similar. You may invent both people.
writing.modelText:
Ben and Ana are on the same repair team.
They call each other every Monday and share the week's jobs.
Ben works as a driver, so he collects the parts.
Ana talks like a manager, but she is not one; she simply knows everybody.
They cover each other's work when one of them is away.
writing.successCriteria: Five sentences. Each other or one another used twice. One sentence with as for a real job. One sentence with like for something similar. Every sentence ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Write the two names and the one thing they both do. Then ask: does the action go both ways? If it does, the sentence takes each other.
writing.extension: Add a sixth sentence with each other's: They know each other's timetable.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 3 — A reply with a suggestion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Somebody in your group writes: The Saturday meeting is too early for me, so I am going to give it up. Write a reply of four sentences. Say their point back in fewer words, make one suggestion with what about or how about, and offer one alternative. You may invent the group.
writing.modelText:
So you are saying that the time is the problem, not the meeting itself.
What about the Wednesday group? It meets at six, and there are two places left.
If Wednesday does not suit you either, how about coming once a month instead?
Tell me which option you prefer and I will pass it on.
writing.successCriteria: Four sentences. One sentence that says their point back in fewer words. One suggestion with what about or how about, followed by a noun or an -ing word. One alternative. No word to after about.
writing.support: Write the suggestion on its own first. Choose the thing you want to suggest. If it is a verb, add -ing. Then put what about or how about in front of it.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence saying what you will do if they turn both options down.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 4 — What we said, in six lines
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write six lines about a conversation, real or invented. Line 1: who you talked to and where. Line 2: their problem. Line 3: your problem. Line 4: the point you both agreed on, starting So you are saying. Line 5: the suggestion that came out of it. Line 6: what you will do next. You may invent every detail.
writing.modelText:
Last Tuesday I talked to a member of the garden team outside the centre.
Her problem is simple: the Saturday team has lost two people and cannot carry on.
My problem is the day, because I work every Saturday until two.
So you are saying you need people, and I am saying I need another day.
Her suggestion was the Wednesday group, because it is smaller and it meets at six.
I will find out this week whether Wednesday still has a place.
writing.successCriteria: Six lines, one for each part above. Line 4 starts with So you are saying. Line 5 holds a suggestion. Line 6 says what you will do next. Every line ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Write line 5 first. A suggestion is easier to write than a summary. Then work backwards and ask what problem the suggestion was for.
writing.extension: Read the six lines out loud, then say the whole conversation back in one sentence.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which two-word verb?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write one verb in each gap. Change the form if you need to.
Use: look after, put off, deal with, carry on, give up, find out, turn down, take over.
1. She ____ her neighbour's cat while he is away.
2. The meeting was ____ until next month.
3. Who ____ complaints in this office?
4. He stopped for a drink of water, then ____ working.
5. I ____ coffee two years ago and I feel better.
6. Ring the desk and ____ what time it opens.
7. They offered me the job, but I ____. (turn down, with the word it)
8. When the manager left, Eva ____ the team. (take over)
activities.answerSummary:
1. looks after 2. put off 3. deals with 4. carried on 5. gave up 6. find out 7. turned it down 8. took over
Eight out of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the word cards you missed. Five or fewer: read all eight word cards again, then do this once more.
Item 7 is the one to check. Turn down splits around it, so the answer is turned it down, never turned down it.
activities.soloPath: Cover the verb list with your hand for the first four items. Uncover it only if you are stuck.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 2 — The talk verbs
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Match each verb to what it does. Write the number and the letter.
Verbs:
1. mention
2. explain
3. describe
4. respond
5. interrupt
6. clarify
7. summarise
8. comment
What it does:
a. Say what something is like.
b. Say a long thing again in a few words.
c. Say it quickly, in passing, without stopping on it.
d. Start talking before the other person has finished.
e. Answer what the other person has just said.
f. Make it clear how or why.
g. Say the same thing again in clearer words, because you were not understood.
h. Say what you think about something.
activities.answerSummary:
1 c, 2 f, 3 a, 4 e, 5 d, 6 g, 7 b, 8 h.
Eight out of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the two word cards you missed and write one sentence with each.
The pair people mix up is explain and clarify. Explain is the first time. Clarify is the second time, after the other person has not understood.
activities.soloPath: Do it in pencil and check. Then cover the answers and do it again from memory tomorrow.

activities.title: Practice 3 — People together
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: partner, team, member, community, relationship, contact, stranger, acquaintance.
1. I have never met him. He is a complete ____.
2. She is a ____ of the garden team.
3. Give me your number, so I have a ____ at the office.

8. They have worked together for ten years and they have a good working ____.

assignments.title: A conversation that does not stop
assignments.instructions:
Make one recording and write one short card. You may invent every person and every detail.
Part 1. The recording, about two minutes.
Hold a conversation about joining a group, taking a course, or a problem at work.
Record both sides yourself: say a line, then answer it as the other person. If somebody is with you, they can take the second part instead.
Use at least four open questions, and not the same one twice.
Use two suggestions with what about or how about, one with a noun and one with an -ing word.
Use three of the two-word verbs, and put it or them in the right place at least once.
Use one sentence with as and one with like.
End by saying the other person's point back, starting So you are saying.
Play it back with a pen in your hand and count each item in the list above.
If a count is short, record it again.
Part 2. The card.
Write six lines with the layout of Writing 4: who, their problem, your problem, the agreed point, the suggestion, what you will do next.
Use each other or one another once.
Under the card, write one line that starts: This shows I can …
Check the card against the four criteria for Writing 4 before you finish.

quizzes.correctAnswer: Why did you put it off?
